Drug Arrests Up, Sentences Down
March 13, 2000

Increase in Marijuana Cases Drives Numbers, Say Experts

WASHINGTON (APBnews.com) -- Federal drug laws are leading to an increased number of arrests and convictions, but prison time served by drug offenders is dropping, a fact some observers say is related to the increased number of marijuana cases now showing up in federal courts.

All three of the federal government's leading anti-drug agencies, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the Customs Service and the FBI, approached the end of the last decade with record numbers of arrests and convictions for drugs, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), a research institute at Syracuse University that studies federal prosecution and law enforcement activities.

Using the agencies' own numbers, TRAC found that the DEA won 10,048 drug convictions in 1998 -- the last year for which data are available -- compared with 9,555 drug convictions in 1992. The Customs Service, now the second-most active anti-drug force in the country, nearly doubled its drug convictions, from 2,692 in 1992 to 4,730 in 1998. The FBI's drug convictions rose from 1,925 to 3,253 in the same period.

But between those same years, the average federal prison sentence fell 22 percent, from 86 months to 67 months.

'Safety valve' effect cited

In a statement, the U.S. Justice Department acknowledged TRAC's findings, but emphasized the increased court activity overall.

" We have been aware of this trend for some time. It is worth noting that the number of drug defendants sentenced has increased by 21 percent during this period, " according to the statement.

The Justice Department explained the drop in sentence lengths by citing the increased number of defendants who pleaded guilty and who confessed, providing trafficking information that investigators found useful. Both factors can win defendants shorter sentences.

The Justice Department also pointed to changes in sentencing laws. In 1994, Congress passed a " safety valve " that allowed judges to give first-time, nonviolent federal drug convicts a reduction in mandatory minimum prison sentences. Instead of an automatic five-year sentence, eligible defendants could get half that time.

" It took a couple years for the effect to become apparent, but what's been demonstrated there, which is what many people had suspected, is that there are considerable numbers of low-level drug offenders in the federal system, and judges have taken advantage of the safety valve to give them less time, " said Marc Mauer, the assistant director of the Sentencing Project, a nonprofit group that opposes mandatory minimum drug laws.

33 percent of cases from cannibis'

The increase in marijuana cases, which carry shorter sentences than other drugs, might also help explain the drop.

Marijuana cases in 1998 accounted for 33.9 percent of all federal drug convictions, while 27.9 percent of convictions were for powder cocaine; 16.6 percent crack; 10.7 percent methamphetamine; and 7.7 percent heroin. Other drugs made up 3.2 percent of the cases.

" Thirty-three percent of cases from cannabis -- that is astonishingly high, " said Mark A.R. Kleiman, a professor at the University of California Los Angeles who studies drug enforcement. " It looks to me what's happened is that the case mix has moved away from cocaine to heroin to marijuana. Of course you'll get a shorter sentence. "

The surge in Customs Service cases, two-thirds of which involve marijuana, also may have contributed to the drop in sentence lengths. In 1998, Customs was responsible for about 21 percent of all drug convictions; in 1992, it accounted for 14 percent.

" It seems to me to be an awful mistake, " Kleiman said. " With methamphetamines and heroin both surging in the population, if I had a limited enforcement capacity, that's where I'd put it. "

(MarijuanaNews note: I seldom agree with Kleiman, a " moderate " prohibitionist, but he does not recognize that, so long as marijuana is illegal, it will absorb much of the criminal justice resources that could be better spent anywhere else.)

FBI target: 'large cartels'

But Customs defended its performance. While improved staffing techniques and new technology -- such as X-ray machines to scan truck interiors at border crossings -- have led to increased arrests and convictions, Customs still has little control over what type of drugs it seizes, officials said.

" We see incredible amounts of pot coming through the border these days, " said Dean Boyd, a Customs spokesman. " It's unbelievable. But the fact that we're seizing a lot of it doesn't mean we're targeting pot. We don't know what we're going to find when we open the car. "

But according to the FBI, year-to-year numbers may not accurately reflect the long-term success of the FBI's primary task: the destruction of large, international drug trafficking networks.

" The FBI seeks to dismantle major national and international drug organizations at the top, " said Dave Miller, an FBI spokesman. " While your numbers may go up or down one year or another, what we're after are the large cartels. We may be making great progress, and that particular issue isn't reflected in a statistical count in court. "

Hans H. Chen is an APBnews.com staff writer (hans.chen@apbnews.com).
